tldr: By combining silicone nubs with piezoresistive conductive fabric, researchers have developed a 6 mm thin flexible tactile sensor that measures both normal and shear forces. It can be built in-house using everyday tools like 3D printers and a vacuum chamber, achieving a remarkably low cost of under 35 USD per unit.
hero_caption: VecTile mounted on the surface of a flexible Fin-Ray finger while inserting a power plug into an outlet. The matrix colors indicate normal compressive forces, while the white arrows represent the magnitude and direction of shear forces caused by slippage or tilting, capturing complex fingertip contact states in real time.
overview:
For robots to grasp and manipulate objects with human-like dexterity, tactile sensing is indispensable for capturing contact details that vision alone cannot provide. Shear force, which acts parallel to the contact surface, is especially critical for detecting the onset of slip and maintaining stable grasps. However, existing camera-based or magnetic tactile sensors are rigid and bulky, while conventional thin, flexible sensors typically only measure normal forces.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed VecTile, a flexible, thin tactile array that measures 3-axis forces at each taxel. Its mechanism is simple and elegant: a piezoresistive conductive fabric sits on top of a flexible printed circuit (FPC), overlaid with small silicone nubs. When contact causes lateral shear, the nub tilts like a lever, shifting the balance of pressure across four underlying electrode quadrants. By measuring this differential, normal and shear forces can be cleanly separated and estimated.

Through finite element analysis (FEA) and real-world evaluations with a UR5e robot arm, the authors showed that a 3.0 mm nub height achieves high recovery accuracy, with RMSEs of 0.39 N for normal force and 0.16 N for shear force. Furthermore, the sensor maintains accuracy when bent onto curved surfaces, and a simple manual calibration taking only about five minutes is sufficient for practical use.

In hardware demonstrations, VecTile enabled a sharp scalpel to detect minute shear forces and retract reflexively before popping an inflated balloon. It also substantially improved a Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion task, boosting success rates from 48% with vision alone to 88% when shear tactile feedback was included, clearly proving its practical utility.
contributions: Proposed a flexible, 6 mm thin tactile array capable of independently measuring 3-axis forces (normal plus two shear directions) at each taxel.
Clarified and validated the mechanical lever principle—converting shear forces into differential normal pressure signals via tilting nubs—using both finite element analysis and hardware experiments.

Achieved high reproducibility without expensive specialized equipment, costing under 35 USD per unit (under 15 USD with a cheaper microcontroller) using standard 3D printers and hobbyist vacuum chambers.

Demonstrated conformal fit to curved surfaces, established a fast manual calibration procedure, and validated practical performance in balloon puncture avoidance and Diffusion Policy-guided plug insertion.

sections.heading: Why Robot Hands Need Flexible Skin That Senses Slip
sections.summary: Tactile sensors are essential for understanding friction, stiffness, and contact states that vision misses. However, measuring normal force alone is not enough to assess grasp stability and slippage. There is a strong need for an array that measures shear force, fits curved surfaces, and is cheap to repair when damaged. VecTile meets all these needs.
sections.details:
In robotic manipulation, touch is a critical sensory modality for directly perceiving force interactions, friction, and stiffness. Yet, most setups only measure normal forces directed straight into the contact surface. In practical grasping and manipulation, knowing the magnitude and direction of shear (tangential) forces is essential for preventing slip and guiding fine contact corrections.

Furthermore, robot fingertips are frequently curved or made from soft grippers, making a flexible "tactile skin" form factor ideal. But because contact sensors face constant wear and tear, high replacement costs and difficult repairs severely hinder real-world deployment.

Looking at existing sensors, optical camera-based systems like GelSight or magnetic sensors provide rich 3D contact data, but their rigid housings make them bulky. Conversely, thin and soft capacitive or piezoresistive sheets conform well to curved surfaces, but typically only capture normal forces. Until now, sensors that simultaneously offer 3-DoF force sensing, flexibility, and low cost have been virtually nonexistent.

VecTile fills this gap as a 6 mm thin, $4\times 4$ flexible tactile array. Taxels are spaced at a 10 mm pitch, and each one independently reads a 3-DoF force vector. Including its readout electronics, the complete system costs under 35 USD to build, operating at a high sampling rate of 343 Hz with an end-to-end latency of only around 25 ms.

sections.heading: Neither Optical Nor Magnetic: A Thin, Flexible Third Way
sections.summary: While optical and magnetic tactile sensors offer high accuracy, their rigid structures make them difficult to conform to curved geometries. Prior research has explored using nubs to convert shear into normal force, but complex microfabrication hindered lab prototyping. VecTile adopts a simplified design that anyone can build in a standard lab.
sections.details:
Prominent 3-axis tactile sensors include camera-based systems such as GelSight and DIGIT. These track elastomer surface deformations with an internal camera and estimate 3-axis forces using machine learning. While they offer high spatial resolution, they require rigid housings to accommodate cameras, lighting, and optical paths, making fingertips bulky.

Another family relies on magnets and Hall-effect sensors (such as eFlesh and ReSkin). They infer deformation from magnetic displacement and can be made compact, but they still require active electronic boards beneath the sensing surface. This makes bending the entire array or scaling it across large, complex surfaces difficult.

Thin piezoresistive or capacitive sheets, on the other hand, provide excellent flexibility, but simple flat designs only capture normal pressure. To address this, prior work placed "nubs" on the surface to mechanically convert lateral shear forces into differential vertical pressures via a lever mechanism. However, past attempts required spin-coating silicone onto substrates, delicate etching, or multi-layer alignments that were out of reach for everyday lab prototyping.

VecTile takes this nub conversion mechanism and translates it into an ultra-practical design: it uses standard outsourced flexible printed circuits (FPCs) and simple silicone casting in 3D-printed molds, making it readily accessible to any robotics lab.

sections.heading: Tilting Nubs Sense Force: Low-Cost, DIY Hardware Design
sections.summary: Each taxel features an electrode split into four quadrants, layered with silver-fiber conductive fabric and a silicone nub. Normal and shear forces acting on the nub are mechanically decoupled into quadrant sum and difference values. The entire device can be fabricated cheaply using 3D-printed molds and off-the-shelf adhesives without cleanroom tools.
sections.details:
### III-A Sensing Element and Readout Circuit
VecTile consists of 16 taxels arranged in a $4\times 4$ array on an FPC. Crucially, each round taxel is divided into four pie-shaped quadrants. Each quadrant contains an electrode pair, wired into an $8\times 8$ matrix (8 rows of outer electrodes and 8 columns of inner electrodes). A layer of silver-fiber conductive fabric (TEK Silver Fiber 75D), whose resistance drops under applied pressure, sits on top.

Typical piezoresistive sensors sandwich the conductive layer between top and bottom electrode sheets. Instead, VecTile places both positive and negative electrode traces on the same FPC surface, flowing current laterally through the conductive fabric. This eliminates the need for sub-millimeter alignment between two facing sheets. To prevent cross-talk and saturation caused by sneak currents when multiple points are pressed, a transimpedance amplifier (LM358) circuit maintains non-selected columns at virtual ground (0 V). An Arduino Nano reads the values, streaming 64-byte frames at a high rate of approximately 343 Hz.

### III-B Nub Lever Mechanism and Finite Element Analysis
A cast silicone dome-shaped nub covers each taxel. A normal force $F_z$ compresses the nub downward, uniformly decreasing the electrical resistance across all four quadrants. When a lateral shear force $F_x$ or $F_y$ is applied, the nub tilts like a lever, increasing pressure on the leading quadrant while relieving pressure on the trailing quadrant. Thus, the total sum ($\Sigma$) represents normal force, while the difference ($D$) between opposing quadrants represents shear force, yielding a clean, mechanical decoupling.

To validate this mechanism, the authors conducted large-deformation static finite element analysis (FEA) in ANSYS. Under 1–5 N normal loads and up to 1 N shear loads, simulations confirmed that normal force changes project almost exclusively onto the sum metric $\Sigma$, while shear force changes project onto the difference metric $D$. Because the responses remain orthogonal, the 3-axis force can be uniquely recovered. Furthermore, sweeping the nub height from 0.6 mm to 3.0 mm revealed that taller nubs provide a longer lever arm, drastically boosting shear force sensitivity (gain).

### III-C Fabrication Procedure
A key strength of VecTile is that it requires no cleanroom equipment. PLA molds are printed on a consumer 3D printer (Bambu Lab P1S), filled with silicone rubber (Dragon Skin 30), and degassed in a sub-$150 hobbyist vacuum chamber. A dummy plate mimicking the FPC thickness is inserted into the mold, producing a recessed pocket that perfectly fits the FPC and conductive fabric after curing.

Adhesion also involves clever practical choices. The FPC and conductive fabric are tacked down using cyanoacrylate (superglue) dotted away from active electrode surfaces. However, because cyanoacrylate hardens silicone and destroys flexibility, the fabric and silicone nub layer are bonded using a thin layer of the same uncured silicone. This preserves flexibility throughout the entire sensor. Total material costs are approximately 34.67 USD per unit including the readout board, and this can be reduced to under 15 USD with a cheaper microcontroller.

Each taxel consists of four electrode quadrants, with current flowing laterally through the conductive fabric. (B) Pure normal load compresses all four quadrants uniformly, whereas lateral shear tilts the nub, creating a differential signal between opposing electrodes.

(A) Pressure distributions under normal and shear forces, and their mapping into sum $\Sigma$ and difference $D$ spaces, illustrating clean orthogonal decoupling. (B) Increasing nub height substantially raises shear force sensitivity (gain) without compromising normal force transmission.

sections.heading: Tuning Nub Height: Physical Testing and Fast Calibration
sections.summary: Using a robot arm and a reference force/torque sensor, four sensors with different nub heights were evaluated. As predicted by simulations, the 3.0 mm nub provided the highest shear sensitivity, enabling accurate force recovery via a quadratic polynomial. A model calibrated flat transferred directly to curved surfaces, and a five-minute manual rub-down calibration proved effective.
sections.details:
### IV-A Piezoresistive Layer Characterization
Before adding silicone nubs, the baseline properties of the conductive fabric were evaluated on an ATI Mini40 force/torque (F/T) sensor. Applying normal loads to individual quadrants using an indentation pin showed that sensitivity saturates beyond roughly 1.25 N per quadrant (around 5 N across an entire taxel). Based on this, the operational characterization range was set to 1–5 N normal force.

### IV-B & C Nub Height Comparison and Force Recovery
Next, automated contact and shear experiments were performed using a UR5e robot arm equipped with an indentation probe and an F/T sensor across four sensors with nub heights $h = 0.6, 1.0, 2.0,$ and $3.0$ mm. Under normal preloads of 1–5 N, the probe was translated 2 mm laterally along eight directions (at 45-degree intervals), collecting 348,800 data points.

Empirical measurements matched FEA predictions closely. While the sum metric $\Sigma$ under normal loads remained largely constant across all nub heights, the shear difference metric $D$ under 1 N shear rose from 34.2 counts for the 0.6 mm nub to 101.6 counts for the 3.0 mm nub—nearly a three-fold increase.

To recover 3-axis forces $(F_x, F_y, F_z)$ from each taxel's four ADC quadrant outputs, a quadratic polynomial regression model was fitted. Cross-validation across unseen shear directions showed that the 3.0 mm nub achieved a normal force RMSE of 0.39 N and a shear force RMSE of 0.16 N. In contrast, the 0.6 mm nub had a shear RMSE of 0.29 N, confirming the advantage of taller nubs.

Furthermore, when the sensor was mounted onto convex and concave fixtures with a radius of curvature $R = 85$ mm, the polynomial model calibrated on a flat surface still predicted forces accurately: RMSE increases were limited to an average of 0.05 N for normal force and 0.06 N for shear force. This confirms that VecTile can be calibrated flat and deployed on curved fingertips without recalibration.

### IV-D Practical Fast Manual Calibration
Spending hours gathering automated calibration data with a robot arm is impractical for everyday robotics workflows. Instead, the authors evaluated a quick manual calibration: resting VecTile on an F/T sensor, a user presses and circles each taxel with a finger for about 10 presses of 0.55 s each, taking just a few minutes (around 1,400 samples total).

This fast calibration retained strong accuracy, achieving normal RMSE of 0.43 N and shear RMSE of 0.22 N. Cross-correlation between reference F/T values and VecTile estimates showed an end-to-end latency of roughly 25 ms. In multi-taxel tests involving random presses with a palm or multiple fingers, total force errors remained modest: 0.71 N for normal force and 0.43 N for shear force.

sections.heading: Unpopped Balloons and Plug Insertion: Dexterity via Shear Sensing
sections.summary: VecTile was mounted onto flexible Fin-Ray grippers for two real-world manipulation tasks. First, a reflexive control loop used shear feedback to retract a sharp scalpel before puncturing a balloon. Second, integrating 3-axis tactile feedback into a Diffusion Policy increased the success rate of power-plug insertion from 48% to 88%.
sections.details:
### V-A Scalpel-Balloon Reflex Experiment
To showcase sensitivity to delicate shear forces, a gripper held a sharp surgical scalpel and advanced it into an inflated balloon at 5 mm/s. In preliminary baseline tests where the balloon was popped intentionally, fingertip sensors experienced a shear change of approximately 0.5 N right before the puncture.

Setting a reflexive retraction threshold of just 0.1 N of shear change per taxel, the robot backed away immediately upon detection. Over 20 consecutive trials, the robot caught the subtle lateral catch of the blade on the rubber surface and retracted safely without popping the balloon once. In contrast, using normal force as the trigger failed completely: the blade pierced the rubber membrane before normal force reached its threshold, popping the balloon in 100% of trials. This highlights how shear force is far more sensitive for rapid contact detection.

### V-B Visuotactile Diffusion Policy for Plug Insertion
Next, VecTile was evaluated in an insertion task involving a UK 3-pin power plug, which entails complex contact changes. VecTile was mounted onto the curved surface of flexible Fin-Ray fingers 3D-printed from TPU. Visual streams from two cameras (wrist and exterior) were combined with tactile arrays from both fingers (96 dimensions total, compressed to 16 dimensions via PCA) and fed into a Diffusion Policy.

The policy was trained on 84 human teleoperated demonstrations and tested on unseen socket locations. The results demonstrated substantial performance gains:
- Vision-only: 48% success rate (12/25)
- Vision + Normal force only: 64% success rate (16/25)
- Vision + 3-Axis VecTile tactile: 88% success rate (22/25)

Adding shear forces dramatically improved recovery behaviors from misalignments. When the plug's ground pin catches obliquely against the socket bevel, the contact point is occluded from the cameras, but VecTile clearly senses the torsional shear pattern. Guided by this shear signal, the policy autonomously carried out fine wiggling motions to find the holes and press straight in, exhibiting human-like dexterity. Despite repeated heavy interactions, the sensor surface—costing only about 4 USD—suffered no visible damage.

(A) Balloon puncture avoidance: detecting a shear force change of just 0.1 N triggers instant retraction, preventing the scalpel from puncturing the balloon. (B) Diffusion Policy-guided plug insertion: even when the socket is visually occluded, fingertip shear force vectors reveal contact jams and tilting, allowing the policy to search and smoothly complete insertion.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Towards Cut-to-Fit Tactile Skins
sections.summary: VecTile solves the long-standing trade-off between flexibility, 3-DoF force sensing, and low cost through its nub lever mechanism and clever circuit layout. Future work will focus on expanding dynamic range, evaluating long-term durability, and creating modular cut-to-fit skins.
sections.details:
VecTile introduces a flexible tactile array that leverages passive silicone nubs to translate shear forces into differential quadrant pressures, enabling accurate 3-axis force measurements at each taxel. Costing under 35 USD per unit and requiring no cleanroom equipment, its high accessibility is an exciting prospect for the robotics research community.

The design was rigorously validated through FEA simulations and physical testing, demonstrating robustness to curved surfaces, a fast five-minute manual calibration, and clear task improvements in balloon preservation and plug insertion.

Several limitations remain to be addressed. The current conductive fabric saturates around 5 N per taxel, requiring wider dynamic range for handling heavier objects. In addition, the inherent hysteresis, drift, and long-term mechanical degradation of piezoresistive fabrics and silicones require systematic evaluation.

The authors note they are already developing a new cut-to-fit VecTile design that can be trimmed with scissors into custom shapes. Future work will also include benchmarking against high-end commercial tactile sensors and establishing unified tactile representations that generalize across varied sensor hardware.

takeaways: Converting shear forces into differential normal pressures using nubs is an exceptionally practical way to achieve flexible 3-axis tactile sensing without complex multi-axis transducers.
Without expensive cleanrooms or specialized equipment, reliable tactile arrays can be built using standard commercial FPCs, desktop 3D-printed molds, and hobbyist vacuum chambers.
A polynomial force-recovery model calibrated while flat retains usable accuracy on curved surfaces (down to R = 85 mm) without requiring recalibration.
In robot imitation learning (such as Diffusion Policy), shear feedback clearly signals jams and tilts that vision alone misses, dramatically boosting manipulation success rates.
limitations: Piezoresistive sensitivity begins to saturate around 5 N per taxel (1.25 N per quadrant), making it unsuitable for heavy-duty grasping or high-load manipulation as currently designed.
Inherent piezoresistive and elastomer behaviors—such as hysteresis, temporal signal drift, and long-term wear or adhesive degradation—have not yet been quantitatively characterized.
The current prototype is limited to a 10 mm pitch $4\times 4$ array (16 taxels), which lacks the spatial resolution of optical tactile sensors (like GelSight) for fine geometric texture recognition.
